Par exemple, veiller à se lever régulièrement, bouger les épaules doucement en faisant des rotations, ajuster la hauteur de ton siège et de ton écran pour qu’ils soient à un niveau confortable.

fetched_contents.text: The Ultimate 'Deskercise' Routine: Stretches for the Office If you’re feeling stiff and uncomfortable while working at a sedentary job, there are exercises you can do without even leaving your desk that can leave you feeling refreshed. Work-related health problems aren’t just limited to heavy manufacturing or construction. They can occur in all types of industries and work environments, including office spaces. Staying in one position while performing repetitive motions is typical of a desk job, but it may not be the most comfortable or best for your health, especially over long periods. The habits we build at our desk, especially while sitting, can contribute to discomfort and health issues, including: * neck and shoulder pain * obesity * musculoskeletal disorders * stress * lower back pain * carpal tunnel The good news is that moving or stretching is a buildable habit. A simple way to make sure you include movement in your daily life is to set a timer to remind you to take a quick walk or stretch. If you’re pressed for time, there are even certain stretches you can do at your desk. Keep reading for some simple exercises you can do without leaving your chair. Remember to breathe normally throughout the stretches, and never hold your breath. With each stretch, you may find yourself more flexible. Don’t go further than is comfortable. Top tip: Exhale as you lean into the stretch for a greater range of motion. This article is Day 2 of Healthline’s 30 Days of Movement Challenge. Learn more about how you can build long-lasting fitness habits through quick and accessible exercises by following the Challenge. Stretching out your arms Triceps stretches 1. Raise your arm and bend it so that your hand is reaching toward the opposite shoulder. 2. Use your other hand and pull your elbow toward your head. 3. Hold for 10 to 30 seconds. 4. Repeat on the other side. Overhead reach stretch 1. Extend one arm up above your head. 2. Reach toward the opposite side. 3. Hold for 10 to 30 seconds. 4. Repeat on the other side. Stretching out your torso Shoulder, or pectoralis stretch 1. Clasp hands behind your back. 2. Push the chest outward, and raise your chin. 3. Hold the pose for 10 to 30 seconds. Forward stretch This stretch is also known as the rhomboid upper or upper back stretch. 1. Clasp your hands in front of you and lower your head in line with your arms. 2. Press forward and hold for 10 to 30 seconds. Stretching out your legs and knees Hip and knee flexion stretch 1. Hug one knee at a time, pulling it toward your chest. 2. Hold the pose for 10 to 30 seconds. 3. Alternate for the other leg. Hamstrings stretch 1. Remaining seated, extend one leg outward and prop your foot on a second chair. 2. Bend forward from your waist. 3. Hold for 10 to 30 seconds. 4. Repeat on the other side. Note: Be sure to do this one leg at a time, as doing this exercise with both legs out can cause back issues. Head and shoulder stretches Shoulder shrug 1. Raise both shoulders at once up toward the ears. 2. Drop them and repeat 10 times each direction. Neck stretches 1. Relax and lean your head forward. 2. Slowly roll toward one side and hold for 10 seconds. 3. Repeat on the other side. 4. Relax again and lift your chin back to the starting position. 5. Do this three times in each direction. Upper trap stretch 1. Gently pull your head toward each shoulder until you feel a light stretch. 2. Hold the pose for 10 to 15 seconds. 3. Alternate each side. Other ways to get moving Move to a new position throughout the day to avoid repetitive stress injuries. You may want to try: * standing up while on the phone or eating lunch * getting a flexible standing desk so you can change your position throughout the day * walking laps during quick meetings * getting up from your seat every hour and walking around the office Ask your manager or human resources department about ergonomic furniture.

fetched_contents.text: 5 Back and Neck Stretches to Do Every Day Here are five simple stretches to do throughout your day to help prevent and decrease neck and back pain. Please note that these stretches are for healthy people without existing back or neck conditions. They should not cause any pain when done correctly. Always consult with your doctor before starting any new exercise program. Stretches for Your Back Trunk Rotation * Lying on your back, bend both knees, keeping your feet flat on the bed or the floor. * Move your knees slowly from side to side so that you feel a stretch in your torso. * Keep your shoulders in place and do not lift them up as your knees rotate. * Hold the stretch for 3 to 5 seconds in each direction. Repeat this stretch 10 to 15 times. Slouch Overcorrect * Sit in a chair and allow yourself to slouch completely. * Relax for 2 to 3 seconds in this position and then draw yourself upright, accentuating the curve of your lower back as much as possible. This is the “extreme,” or exaggerated, version of the correct sitting posture. * Hold this position for 2 to 3 seconds and then return to the fully relaxed position. * Repeat this stretch 10 to 15 times. Standing Lumbar Extension * Stand upright, close to a stable surface that you can use to steady yourself if needed. * Position your feet at least hips' width apart. * Support your lower back by placing your hands on the small of your back with fingertips pointing downward so that they meet in the center of your spine. * Slowly bend backwards at the waist as far as you comfortably can, using your hands to keep you steady and keeping your knees straight. * Hold this position for 1 to 2 seconds and then return to the starting position. * Repeat this stretch 10 times. Stretches for Your Neck Neck Retraction * This can be performed in a seated or standing position. Start by looking straight ahead and allowing yourself to relax. * Keep your chin tucked down slightly and move your head slowly backward until it is pulled back as far as you can without straining or feeling any pain. * Continue looking straight ahead, being careful not to tilt the head forward or backward while performing this stretch. * Maintain this position for 3 to 5 seconds and then return to the starting position. * Repeat this stretch 10 to 15 times. Neck Rotation * This stretch can be performed in a seated or standing position. Starting by looking straight ahead and allowing yourself to relax. * Keep your chin tucked down slightly and move your head slowly backward until it is pulled back as far as you can without straining or feeling any pain. * Turn your head gently to the right, and then gently to the left. Remember not to strain your neck or push yourself to the point that you feel pain. * Hold the stretch for 2 to 3 seconds before moving your head to the opposite side. * Repeat this stretch 10 times in each direction, two times a day. Context for why these stretches may help and when to seek further care

Prolonged sitting posture causes shoulder tension primarily by creating repetitive strain on the neck, upper back, and shoulder muscles. The evidence repeatedly ties tight shoulders to sitting for extended periods, poor posture, and overuse, with Healthline explaining that tight shoulders can be caused by sitting for extended periods, incorrect sleeping positions, and injuries, plus weak muscles and incorrect alignment [N2-F2]. Healthline also notes that regular shoulder and neck stretches over four weeks helped reduce neck and shoulder pain in office workers, supporting the idea that stretches can be useful when tension is musculoskeletal and not due to an acute injury or underlying condition [N2-F2]. Similarly, MyHealth Alberta states that exercises for the upper back can help reduce stiffness and discomfort caused by prolonged sitting, and that stretches should not cause pain when done correctly [N4-F4].

Stretches are useful as a first-line self-care measure when the tension is likely muscular or postural, especially if the patient can do them without pain. The evidence suggests that stretches can help loosen and strengthen shoulder muscles, increase flexibility, and prevent injury [N2-F2][N4-F4]. However, stretches are not a substitute for professional care if the pain is intense, lasting, or accompanied by red flags such as radiation, swelling, numbness, or weakness. The evidence explicitly advises consulting a doctor or physiotherapist if stretches do not help, or if the problem persists, and notes that stretches should not be used if they cause pain [N4-F4][N2-F2].

Additional ergonomic and movement tips for daily use include frequent movement and posture adjustments. Healthline recommends taking quick walks or stretches, setting a timer, and breaking long sitting periods with movement [N1-F1]. Healthline also suggests changing positions throughout the day, using ergonomic furniture, and avoiding repetitive strain by standing up while on the phone or eating lunch [N1-F1]. MyHealth Alberta similarly emphasizes starting exercises slowly, easing off if pain occurs, and consulting a healthcare provider for personalized guidance [N4-F4]. Together, these sources support a broader self-care strategy: stretches are helpful alongside regular movement, good posture, and ergonomic adjustments, not a standalone solution [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

2. **Upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck**  
   **Posture:** Sit in a firm chair or stand tall with your arms at shoulder height and your chin slightly tucked [N4-F4].

Mechanics and safety of stretching for upper back and neck

Each stretch targets specific muscles and tissues. The upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck primarily targets the upper trapezius, rhomboids, and the posterior neck and upper back, with the posture cue of pulling the shoulder blades apart emphasizing the mid-back and scapular region [N4-F4][N4-R2]. The cross-arm stretch targets the pectoralis minor and upper back muscles, with the action of stretching the arm across the body and pulling the shoulder forward helping to open the chest and relieve tightness in the anterior shoulder girdle [N2-F2][N4-R3]. The shoulder shrug and neck roll target the levator scapulae, trapezius, and neck rotators, while also affecting the surrounding fascia and posture-related tension patterns [N2-F2][N1-F1].

To avoid overstretching or compensatory movement, the evidence repeatedly stresses starting slowly, easing off if pain occurs, and keeping posture neutral [N4-F4][N4-R3]. For example, the upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck should be done with the chin slightly tucked and the arms clamped in front of the body, avoiding forward head or shoulder elevation [N4-F4]. The cross-arm stretch should keep the shoulders relaxed and not let them rise toward the ears [N4-R3]. The shoulder roll should be smooth and controlled, with motion concentrated in the shoulders rather than the neck or torso [N4-F4]. The evidence also warns against pushing through pain, which could indicate an underlying issue or overextension [N4-F4][N2-F2].

Best practices for frequency and repetition are consistent across the sources. Healthline suggests doing stretches multiple times a day in shorter spurts and increasing sets as mobility improves [N2-F2]. MyHealth Alberta recommends starting each exercise slowly, repeating 2 to 4 times for the rhomboid stretch and 8 to 12 times for the wall push-up, and repeating exercises 2 to 4 times for other stretches [N4-F4]. The desk stretches in Healthline also suggest holding poses for 10 to 30 seconds and repeating on the other side when appropriate [N1-F1]. Overall, the safest pattern is to stretch regularly, keep repetitions moderate, and prioritize comfort and controlled movement [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Practical answer to the patient’s question

If you have tight shoulders from prolonged computer work and want three stretches you can do seated at your desk, the evidence supports simple, repeatable exercises that target the neck, upper back, and shoulders. The key is to keep posture neutral, avoid pain, and repeat them several times during the day. The three stretches I’ll describe are:

1. **Shoulder shrug and neck roll**  
2. **Upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck**  
3. **Cross-arm stretch / chest opener**

### 1. Shoulder shrug and neck roll

**Posture:** Sit upright with your back straight, shoulders relaxed, and hands on your knees or in front of you. For the neck roll, keep your chin slightly tucked and avoid letting your head tilt forward or backward during the stretch [N3-F3].  

**How to do it:**  
- Raise both shoulders up toward your ears.  
- Hold briefly at the top.  
- Drop your shoulders back down.  
- Repeat 10 times [N2-F2].  
- Then roll your shoulders up, back, and down in a smooth circular motion, and then up, forward, and down [N2-F2].  

**Hold time:** The Healthline excerpt says to hold the pose for 10 to 15 seconds during the shoulder shrug, and the neck roll is repeated 10 times in each direction [N1-F1].  

**Why it helps:** This stretch relieves tension in the shoulders and neck by engaging the trapezius, levator scapulae, and surrounding fascia. It is especially practical for desk use because it can be done quickly and repeatedly [N2-F2][N1-F1].  

**Safety notes:** Avoid forcing the movement or holding your breath; stop if pain occurs [N4-F4].

### 2. Upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck

**Posture:** Sit in a firm chair or stand tall with your arms at shoulder height and your chin slightly tucked [N4-F4].  

**How to do it:**  
- Clasp your hands in front of you.  
- Drop your chin toward your chest and reach straight forward to round your upper back.  
- Think about pulling your shoulder blades apart.  
- Hold for 15 to 30 seconds [N4-F4].  

**Hold time:** 15 to 30 seconds [N4-F4].  

**Why it helps:** This stretch targets the upper trapezius, rhomboids, and the posterior neck and upper back. It is useful for office workers because it can be done seated and helps relieve tightness in the upper girdle [N4-F4][N4-R2].  

**Safety notes:** Keep your shoulders relaxed and do not let them rise toward your ears [N4-R3]. Stop if pain occurs [N4-F4].

### 3. Cross-arm stretch / chest opener

**Posture:** Sit upright with your arms relaxed and your back straight. Bring your left arm across your body at chest height, and support your left arm with the elbow crease of your right arm or use your right hand to hold your left arm [N2-F2].  

**How to do it:**  
- Stretch out your shoulder and continue facing forward.  
- Hold the stretch for 30 seconds.  
- Repeat on the opposite side [N2-F2].  

**Hold time:** 30 seconds per side [N2-F2].  

**Why it helps:** This stretch targets the pectoralis minor and upper back muscles, helping to open the chest and relieve tightness in the anterior shoulder girdle [N2-F2][N4-R3].  

**Safety notes:** Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid overextending the neck or spine [N4-R3]. Do not push beyond comfort [N4-F4].

## Why these stretches may help

The evidence explains that prolonged sitting posture causes shoulder tension by creating repetitive strain on the neck, upper back, and shoulder muscles [N2-F2]. Healthline also notes that regular shoulder and neck stretches over four weeks helped reduce neck and shoulder pain in office workers, supporting the idea that stretches can be helpful when the issue is musculoskeletal rather than due to an acute injury or underlying condition [N2-F2]. MyHealth Alberta similarly states that exercises for the upper back can help reduce stiffness and discomfort caused by prolonged sitting, and that stretches should not cause pain when done correctly [N4-F4].

## When to seek further care

Stretches are useful as a first-line self-care measure when the tension is likely muscular or postural, especially if the patient can do them without pain [N2-F2]. However, stretches are not a substitute for professional care if the pain is intense, lasts, or is accompanied by red flags such as radiation, swelling, numbness, or weakness [N4-F4][N2-F2]. The evidence also advises consulting a doctor or physiotherapist if stretches do not help or if the problem persists [N4-F4][N2-F2]. In other words, if the pain worsens or does not improve, it is prudent to seek a professional assessment.

## Additional ergonomic and movement tips

The evidence supports a broader self-care strategy beyond stretching alone. Healthline recommends taking frequent, quick standing and stretching breaks, setting a timer, and breaking long sitting periods with movement [N1-F1]. It also suggests changing positions throughout the day, using ergonomic furniture, and avoiding repetitive strain by standing up while on the phone or eating lunch [N1-F1]. MyHealth Alberta similarly emphasizes starting exercises slowly, easing off if pain occurs, and consulting a healthcare provider for personalized guidance [N4-F4].

## Best practices for frequency and repetition

The safest pattern is to stretch regularly, keep repetitions moderate, and prioritize comfort and controlled movement. Healthline suggests doing stretches multiple times a day in shorter spurts and increasing sets as mobility improves [N2-F2]. MyHealth Alberta recommends starting each exercise slowly, repeating 2 to 4 times for the rhomboid stretch and 8 to 12 times for the wall push-up, and repeating exercises 2 to 4 times for other stretches [N4-F4]. The desk stretches in Healthline also suggest holding poses for 10 to 30 seconds and repeating on the other side when appropriate [N1-F1].

## Bottom line

For your situation—7 hours at the computer, tight shoulders, and pain at the end of the day—these three stretches are practical, safe, and evidence-supported. They can help relieve tension in the neck, upper back, and shoulders while you stay seated. However, if the pain does not improve or gets worse, you should consult a professional healthcare provider [N2-F2][N4-F4]. For best results, combine stretching with regular movement, good posture, and ergonomic adjustments [N1-F1][N4-F4].

2. **Upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck**

**Posture:** Sit upright with your back straight, shoulders relaxed, and hands on your knees or in front of you. For the neck roll, keep your chin slightly tucked and avoid letting your head tilt forward or backward during the stretch [N3-F3].  

**How to do it:**  
- Raise both shoulders up toward your ears.  
- Hold briefly at the top.  
- Drop your shoulders back down.  
- Repeat 10 times [N2-F2].  
- Then roll your shoulders up, back, and down in a smooth circular motion, and then up, forward, and down [N2-F2].  

**Hold time:** The Healthline excerpt says to hold the pose for 10 to 15 seconds during the shoulder shrug, and the neck roll is repeated 10 times in each direction [N1-F1].  

**Why it helps:** This stretch relieves tension in the shoulders and neck by engaging the trapezius, levator scapulae, and surrounding fascia. It is especially practical for desk use because it can be done quickly and repeatedly [N2-F2][N1-F1].  

**Safety notes:** Avoid forcing the movement or holding your breath; stop if pain occurs [N4-F4].

### 2. Upper trapezius stretch / chin tuck

**Posture:** Sit in a firm chair or stand tall with your arms at shoulder height and your chin slightly tucked [N4-F4].  

**How to do it:**  
- Clasp your hands in front of you.  
- Drop your chin toward your chest and reach straight forward to round your upper back.  
- Think about pulling your shoulder blades apart.  
- Hold for 15 to 30 seconds [N4-F4].  

**Hold time:** 15 to 30 seconds [N4-F4].  

**Why it helps:** This stretch targets the upper trapezius, rhomboids, and the posterior neck and upper back. It is useful for office workers because it can be done seated and helps relieve tightness in the upper girdle [N4-F4][N4-R2].  

**Safety notes:** Keep your shoulders relaxed and do not let them rise toward your ears [N4-R3]. Stop if pain occurs [N4-F4].

**Posture:** Sit upright with your arms relaxed and your back straight. Bring your left arm across your body at chest height, and support your left arm with the elbow crease of your right arm or use your right hand to hold your left arm [N2-F2].  

**How to do it:**  
- Stretch out your shoulder and continue facing forward.  
- Hold the stretch for 30 seconds.  
- Repeat on the opposite side [N2-F2].  

**Hold time:** 30 seconds per side [N2-F2].  

**Why it helps:** This stretch targets the pectoralis minor and upper back muscles, helping to open the chest and relieve tightness in the anterior shoulder girdle [N2-F2][N4-R3].

The evidence explains that prolonged sitting posture causes shoulder tension by creating repetitive strain on the neck, upper back, and shoulder muscles [N2-F2]. The safest pattern is to stretch regularly, keep repetitions moderate, and prioritize comfort and controlled movement. For your situation—7 hours at the computer, tight shoulders, and pain at the end of the day—these three stretches are practical, safe, and evidence-supported. They can help relieve tension in the neck, upper back, and shoulders while you stay seated. However, if the pain does not improve or gets worse, you should consult a professional healthcare provider [N2-F2][N4-F4]. For best results, combine stretching with regular movement, good posture, and ergonomic adjustments [N1-F1][N4-F4].
